div.p: SCRA has many resources to offer local hams. Our members have a wide range of knowledge covering everything from the practical to the theoretical - support includes programming handheld radios, setting up amateur radio stations, contest participation guidance, POTA and SOTA activity instruction, emergency communication skills development, and electronics assembly and soldering.
Join SCRA to connect with experienced mentors who can guide skill advancement.

Members can borrow equipment including handheld transceivers, HF rigs, antennas, tuners, analyzers, Morse code keys and training devices, and complete SOTA/POTA kits. Three mobile stations are available for members who volunteer at local community events.

SCRA provides a script for the Tuesday evening Service Net, to help members practice radio communication skills and serve as Net Control. A downloadable PDF script plus supporting documents guide Net Control operators through the weekly net. Members interested in leading the net are encouraged to contact the club president for mentoring.

p.em: The actual PDF script was not carried over in this import - only this description. Re-uploading it as an Odoo attachment is a good follow-up task.

ul.li: Obtain all materials ahead of time
Research the following week's Net Control operator and newsline transmitter
Bolded parenthetical text in the script contains instructions not meant for broadcast
Identify the station every 10 minutes during operations
Release the transmit button between segments, to prevent repeater timeout and allow emergency communications through

div.p: The net script follows a detailed sequence beginning five minutes before the 7pm Tuesday start time:

ul.li: Opening announcement and emergency traffic check
Club membership information
Meeting details (first Wednesday monthly at Luther Burbank Art & Garden Center, Santa Rosa; Zoom option available)
Net traffic handling
Check-in roster for regular participants
Amateur Radio Newsline segment (approximately 20 minutes)
Additional check-ins and closing announcements

div.p: The script concludes by announcing the next week's Net Control operator and newsline transmitter, then formally ends the net.

SCRA Emergency Services exists to provide assistance and resources to all radio operators, and the community, in the event of a major disaster. The club does not directly operate emergency communication nets for agencies - instead it collaborates closely with local groups and conducts training exercises, often partnered with the ARRL-sponsored Amateur Radio Emergency Service (ARES), the City of Santa Rosa's Auxiliary Emergency Communication System (AECS), and the Sonoma County Auxiliary Communication Service (ACS).
SCRA provides training to neighborhood groups interested in emergency communications, covering ham radio, Family Radio Service (FRS), and General Mobile Radio Service (GMRS) operations.
Repeater Access: the SCRA repeater (147.315 MHz) is available to all licensed operators during emergencies and disasters for sharing relevant information.

Storm Watch Net: during severe weather events, SCRA operates a Storm Watch Net at 8:00am, 4:00pm, and 8:00pm on the SCRA repeater (147.315 - PL88.5), or on 147.315 simplex if the repeater fails. All hams are encouraged to monitor and report hazardous conditions.
Rather than a dedicated emergency net, SCRA members are encouraged to:

ul.li: Join the SCRA Service Net every Tuesday at 7:00pm on the SCRA repeater
Join the ARES net every Monday at 7:30pm on the SCRA repeater
Participate in the 10 meter net every Tuesday at 8:30pm on 28.403 MHz

div.p: For more information, contact SCRA at k6son@arrl.net.

During the 2023 flood on the Russian River, GMRS proved invaluable for communities without power, cell service, or landlines. SCRA's Neighborhood Communications Committee works to bridge amateur radio operators with community groups using General Mobile Radio Service.
Family Radio Service (FRS) is a low-power, unlicensed, channelized service with no licence fee. It operates on channels 1-22 but has no repeater capability.

GMRS shares the same channels but offers high-power transmission, full-duplex repeater capability on channels 15-22, and requires an FCC licence ($35 for 10 years, covering family members) with no exam required.

The services are completely interoperable on simplex channels. An unlicensed FRS user with a $10 radio can access a GMRS simplex repeater with permission, providing coverage over roughly a 2-mile diameter. Licensed GMRS users with 5-watt radios ($40-$200) can achieve reliable multi-mile communication.

ul.li: Lower cost and easier access compared to amateur radio
No testing required for GMRS licensing
Family members can share a single GMRS licence at no additional cost
Eight widely available GMRS repeater channels, informally coordinated through mygmrs.com

div.p: Amateur radio offers superior technical performance, but FRS/GMRS's accessibility makes it increasingly attractive for emergency preparedness and community communication.

FRS radios operating at 2 watts or less on channels 1-7 and 15-22, or ½ watt on channels 8-14, require no licence. GMRS radios with higher power and repeater capability do require licensing - a GMRS licence costs $35 for a 10-year term via the FCC.

GMRS licensees may allow family members to operate under their licence - defined as spouse, children, grandchildren, stepchildren, parents, grandparents, stepparents, brothers, sisters, aunts, uncles, nieces, nephews, and in-laws. Club/association members may only use another's licence if that licensee holds grandfathered rights.

ul.li: Channels 1-7: 2W limit (FRS and GMRS)
Channels 8-15: 0.5W limit (FRS and GMRS)
Channels 15-22: 2W limit for FRS; 50W limit for GMRS

div.p: Eight additional frequencies serve as repeater inputs only (identified as RP15-RP22 on some radios).
Repeaters operate only on channels 15-22 and must be owned and controlled by GMRS licensees. FRS users (2W or less) may use GMRS repeaters with owner authorization.

Duplex repeaters receive on one frequency and transmit on another simultaneously, requiring GMRS-capable radios and more complex programming. Simplex repeaters record and echo messages on the same frequency, allowing unlicensed FRS users to access them if permitted.
Closed repeaters require owner permission for use; open repeaters are generally available to authorized operators. Find listings at mygmrs.com.

Sonoma County tests indicate flat-terrain performance of 1W radios is solid to 1 mile, good to 2 miles. Five-watt units achieve solid to 2 miles, good to 4 miles. Hilly terrain varies significantly; coastal 5W radios with roof-mounted antennas can reach 10+ miles to repeaters.

FRS radios require fixed antennas, but GMRS radios permit antenna upgrades, external antennas, and cables for improved range. Radios use inaudible tones to filter incoming transmissions - most offer 38 analog codes, some support 104 digital tones, though this does not eliminate interference from simultaneous transmissions on different codes.

ul.li: Low-cost FRS radios: $10-$40, no licence needed
5W GMRS handhelds: $40-$200, requires licence
40-50W mobile radios: requires separate power supply, antenna cable, and exterior antenna, for maximum range

div.p: Other useful features: scanning, NOAA weather radio, flashlight, USB charging, VOX, monitor button, flotation, vibrate alert, power level selectors, and a locking feature.
GMRS stations must identify at the end of transmissions or a series of transmissions, or at least every 15 minutes. FRS operators aren't required to use call signs.

Regulations allow unlicensed operators to use a licensee's GMRS radio during an emergency, but unlicensed individuals cannot operate their own GMRS equipment even in an emergency - get licensed if you own a GMRS radio.
FRS/GMRS may be used for brief business communications. There is no privacy on these frequencies - assume all transmissions are public, avoid indecent language, and yield to emergency traffic.

For emergency preparedness, consider removing rechargeable batteries and storing fresh batteries separately in your emergency kit. Rotate stored batteries every two years, and never store batteries in radios, as they may leak and damage equipment.
For regulatory details, see 47 CFR 95.1701. Contact SCRA with corrections or updates: mikevdpca@aim.com.
Anything that does not exceed 2 watts is FRS, operating on channels 1-22; anything exceeding 2 watts qualifies as GMRS.

ul.li: Midland LXT 210: 1 watt (channels 1-7, 15-22), ½ watt (channels 8-14)
Motorola Talkabout 5000 & 6400: 1 watt and ½ watt across the same channel groups
Uniden GMRS 540: ½ watt across all channels

div.p: Handheld models range from around $40 (Retevis RT76P) to $169 (Wouxun KG-UV9G PRO), including offerings from Baofeng and other manufacturers. Mobile units cost $200-$250, such as the Baofeng GMRS-50X1 and Midland MXT-400.
Antennas are more important than transmit power, particularly for handheld units. Recommended upgrades:

ul.li: Nagoya NA-701G ($16.99) - GMRS-specific tuning
Smiley 5/8 Slim Duck ($24.50) - noted as superior for handheld use
Mag-mount antennas - for vehicle installation
Laird FG4603 ($133) - for base station setups

img.alt: Cable comparison chart for base station antennas

div.p: SCRA's Neighborhood Communications Committee bridges ham radio operators and community groups using GMRS and FRS - emergency communication alternatives when traditional infrastructure fails.

FRS operates on channels 1-22 as an unlicensed, low-power service requiring no exam or fee. It lacks repeater capability but allows operators to use GMRS simplex repeaters with permission, enabling "last mile" communications over roughly 2-mile zones using inexpensive equipment.

GMRS covers the same channels but offers high-power transmission and full-duplex repeater options on channels 15-22. The service requires an FCC licence ($35 for 10 years) with no exam, and licensees may share their licence with specified family members at no additional cost.

ol.li: Register for an FRN at apps.fcc.gov/coresWeb/publicHome.do
Apply through the FCC ULS at fcc.gov/wireless/.../applyingnew-license

div.p: The licence and callsign typically arrive within hours to one day of submission.

During emergencies, the first GMRS operator on-air becomes the Net Control Operator, establishing a directed emergency net. Responsibilities include assessing communication assets and establishing contact with emergency services, verifying information before broadcasting to prevent misinformation, passing emergency traffic through available resources, and operating 24-hour monitoring with scheduled check-ins every hour during daytime shifts. Only verified information should be passed onto others by the NCO.
Guidance for GMRS operations when facing electrical outages, wildfires, flooding, storms, tsunamis, earthquakes, or other wide-scale disasters.

GMRS provides emergency communication by operating an Emergency Net that collects information, distributes updates to operators, and relays messages between GMRS operators, ham radio operators, first responders, and government authorities.

ul.li: A GMRS volunteer maintains contact lists of potential Net Control Operators (NCOs) with communication-assets data
Training is offered via Zoom sessions to the GMRS community
Operators can pursue FEMA training: ICS 100 and ICS 700 at training.fema.gov
Emergency contact lists for operators, nets, and emergency services are distributed and posted online

div.p: The first GMRS operator on air becomes the initial NCO. Key responsibilities: assess personal communication assets; operate as a directed net with all traffic routed through the NCO; establish contact with ham radio NCOs, particularly through the Fort Ross GMRS repeater; make contact with other operators via radio, phone, cell, or satellite phone; pass emergency message traffic to appropriate recipients.
Upon activation, the NCO announces: "The GMRS Emergency Net is now activated due to [nature of emergency]. My name is [name and call sign]. I am the first GMRS NCO for this event."

ul.li: 2-hour NCO shifts between 0800 and 2400 hours (local time)
8-hour overnight shift from 2400 to 0800 hours
Hourly 10-minute check-ins at the half-hour during daytime shifts
NCO monitors constantly during the day; overnight NCO may sleep with the radio nearby
If severe, overnight shifts can shorten to 2 hours each with hourly check-ins
PG&E Public Safety Power Shutoff updates
CalFire incidents
Timber Cove Fire Department (707-847-3299)
Fort Ross Fire Department (707-847-3184)

div.p: It is critical that only verified information be passed onto others by the NCO. If something reported is not from a verified source or is questionable, the NCO must confirm the truth of the information before it is broadcast. For urgent traffic involving risk to life or property, the NCO uses available resources to route the request to 911 or emergency authorities as quickly as possible.
When the emergency concludes, the NCO announces the net's termination, and GMRS holds a meeting afterward to discuss outcomes and lessons learned.

div.h1: FRS / GMRS Activity in Sonoma County
div.p: This page documents FRS and GMRS repeater activity and emergency communications networks across Sonoma County.
Active GMRS repeaters are organized by region:

ul.li: Coastal Hills: Fort Ross, Timber Cove, and Muniz repeaters
North County: Fitch, Cloverdale, Knight, and Franz repeaters
Lower Russian River: Mt Jackson and Hacienda repeaters
Central and East County: Sonoma Mountain, Los Alamos, and other locations

div.p: West Marin County also has its own set of GMRS repeaters with memory-channel assignments for portable radio programming.

p.em: The original page's detailed frequency/tone tables per repeater were summarized rather than transcribed verbatim in this import - re-fetch the source page directly if the literal table data is wanted.

ul.li: North County operates an active CERT program connecting incident commanders and community leaders through GMRS.
Sebastopol has established the Sebastopol Neighborhood Communications Unit (SNCU) with "quadrant hubs" and FRS for neighborhood-level communications.
Cazadero deployed four new repeaters that performed well during the January 2023 storms.
Petaluma hosts a weekly net on Tuesday evenings at 8:30pm.

div.p: Sebastopol's Map Your Neighborhood program uses a channel plan designating specific FRS/GMRS channels for quadrant-to-hub and hub-to-net-control communications.
Contact the Education Chair at education@sonomacountyradioamateurs.com for ongoing support.
Dave W6IBC has created a programming guide for those needing help configuring this radio model.
Search for new call signs at the FCC database.

All About Circuits educational platform

Ham Radio Outlet, Amateur Electronic Supply, Universal Radio, and Radio Shack.
Regional amateur radio clubs and the national American Radio Relay League (ARRL), with local section information.
Contact information for Sonoma County ARES, AECS, and related emergency communication services - see also Emergency Services.
